title: Signal Delay Time
statement:
A signal is sent from one node of a directed network and forwarded along every outgoing link; find how long until every node has received it.

Contract
- Nodes are numbered `1..nodeCount`. `links[i] = {from, to, delay}` is a one-way link that takes `delay >= 0` time units.
- A node forwards the signal the instant it first receives it, along all its outgoing links at once.
- Return the time at which the last node receives the signal, or `-1` if some node is never reached.
- The source itself receives the signal at time 0, so a network of one node returns 0. Links may repeat and may form cycles. Do not modify `links`.

Examples
- `links = {{1,2,4},{1,3,1},{3,2,2},{2,4,5}}`, `nodeCount = 4`, `source = 1` returns `8` (node 2 at time 3, node 4 at 8).
- `links = {{1,2,3}}`, `nodeCount = 3`, `source = 1` returns `-1`.
- No links, `nodeCount = 1`, `source = 1` returns `0`.
hints: The time a node hears the signal is the length of the shortest path from the source, and the answer is the largest of those shortest paths.
Links have different delays, so plain breadth-first search is wrong: a path with more links can be faster. Settle nodes in order of increasing arrival time (Dijkstra).
Use a min-heap keyed by arrival time and skip stale heap entries. After the search, any node still unreached means -1. Intended complexity: O((V + E) log V) time and O(V + E) space.
inputSyntax: Input: node count, source node, then links as from>to:delay, for example: 4 1 1>2:4 1>3:1 3>2:2 2>4:5
